newsitem.title: USA: CSCE coffee surges in a correction, no news cited.
newsitem.headline: CSCE coffee surges in a correction, no news cited.

text.p: CSCE coffee futures burst higher on Tuesday, with the key May contract gaining a hefty 10 percent on the day in a technical correction to the market's recent downturn, traders said.
After slipping more than 50.00 cents per lb since the market's surge to two-and-a-half year highs earlier this month, traders said the market was due to bounce back.
"It was due for a correction, but nobody expected it to happen in one day -- never mind one hour," one dealer said. "Once it started, nobody was going to sell it on the way up."
Speculators were the main buyers, traders said, with other sectors joining the panicked fray after technical buy orders were activated above 170.00 cents per lb basis May.

May futures jumped 16.40 cents per lb on the day, to close at 179.30 cents -- its highest level in a week -- after ranging from 181.00 to 160.50. Second-position July soared 14.85 cents, to 168.65, while the remaining months finished 9.25 to 13.95 higher.
Some traders said the market's run-up was exacerbated by a dearth of sellers, with many Latin American producers on the sidelines ahead of the long Easter weekend.
"What we saw was a technically inspired rally with origin activity on the slack side," said Prudential Securities analysts Arthur Stevenson. "I do not have any fundamental story."
Traders and analysts widely agreed there was no new fundamental imput responsible for today's run-up.
"There was nothing behind today's move," said Stephen Smith, president of South Futures in Miami. "More than anything, the market proved to itself that it reached a bottom and away we went."
Smith said the market could work higher in the short-term, but if no fresh fundamentals emerged it was likely to falter going into North America's low consumption period.

Other market participants said that the market's fundamentals remained supportive. While a steady recovery of consumer stocks in recent weeks had eased near-term supply concerns, they said the tight scenario was far from over and likely to reassert itself in the coming months.
"There is a realization that we had some coffee coming in and now its going slow down," said Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes. "The producers are well sold."
The day's volume was brisk, at an estimated 14,587 lots, compared with Monday's official tally of 16,770 lots.
